messages.content:
Outcome: Depressive symptoms (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: no effect
Claim: Vitamin D supplementation did not reduce Hamilton D-17 depression scores compared with placebo at 12 weeks in patients with depression.
Sentence: "No significant reduction in depression was seen after vitamin D supplementation compared to placebo at Hamilton (18.4-18.0; p = 0.73 at 12 weeks)."
Measured as: Hamilton D-17 depression score
Population: Outpatients aged 18-65 with mild to severe depression
Intervention: Vitamin D3 70 micrograms daily on top of standard treatment
Comparator: Placebo on top of standard treatment
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: not reported
baseline_vitamin_d_status: mixed

## Study B
Found: benefit
Claim: Vitamin D supplementation reduced depression severity (BDI-II) more than placebo in patients with mild to moderate depression.
Sentence: "At the end point, statistically significant changes were observed only in intervention group as compared with controls including increased 25(OH)D concentration (+ 40.83 ± 28.57 vs. + 5.14 ± 23.44 nmol L-1, P < 0.001) and decreased depression severity (-11.75 ± 6.40 vs. -3.61 ± 10.40, P = 0.003)."
Measured as: depression severity (Beck Depression Inventory-II)
Population: 56 patients aged 18-60 years with mild to moderate depression
Intervention: cholecalciferol 50,000 IU every 2 weeks for 8 weeks
Comparator: placebo
Design: randomized controlled trial
Sample size: 56
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

content.text: {"rationale":"Both are placebo-controlled RCTs of vitamin D in depressed adults, but they use different depression instruments (Hamilton D-17 vs BDI-II) and differ in dose, duration, and population severity.","verdict":"genuine","reason":"outcome_measure","also_differs":["intervention","population"],"detail":"instrument: Hamilton D-17 vs BDI-II; dose: 70 mcg daily vs 50,000 IU fortnightly for 8 weeks; population: outpatients with mild to severe depression vs 56 patients with mild to moderate depression"}
